items.note: Upendra, a Rāṣṭrakūṭa, obtained sovereignty of Mālava c. 808-812 A.D. through Govinda III; successors traced descent from a mythical hero Paramāra.
Dambarasimha's principality and junior Paramāra lines at Abu, Jalor and Bhinmal; the Paramāras split into many small branches.
Malwa rulers' imperial position; realm extended east up to Bhilsa, Hoshangabad and part of Sagor District.
Dhārā the chief city of Malwa, rebuilt in early 11th century and made royal residence.
Both the Udayapur Praśasti and Navasāhasāṅka-carita say Upendra, first king, was a great-valour king famed for sacrifices; praśasti says he reduced taxes.
Kṛṣṇarāja of Muñja's grants identified with Upendra on Hall's view, since the Udayapur Praśasti names no Kṛṣṇarāja.
Upendra began rule between 808 and 812 A.D., provisionally 809-810; about 27 years per generation to Siyaka II.
Udayapur Praśasti gives the succession Upendra, Vairisimha I, Siyaka I, Vākpati I; Padmagupta confirms a number of rulers between.
Vaidya calls the praśasti's account of these three kings conventional; the author finds no ground for that assertion.
Vairisimha I succeeded about 836-7 A.D.; brother Dambarasimha received Vāgada as feudatory.
Verse 10 of the Udayapur Praśasti describes Vākpati I; a panegyric of the poet, implying control of Avanti.
Vairisimha II succeeded c. 917-18 A.D.; early rulers were subordinates of the Rāṣṭrakūṭas and Paramāra rise depended on Pratihāra and Rāṣṭrakūṭa decline.

reject_reason: Pratihara/Rashtrakuta military background (Mahipala); no bearing on Udaypur or Paramara units

items.note: Malwa not annexed to Kanauj before this time, but Pratihāra supremacy asserted; Partabgarh inscription of 946 A.D. names Mādhava governor of Ujjain.
Dethroned Vairisimha II, in exile among the Rāṣṭrakūṭas, revived Paramāra rule in Malwa and expelled the last Pratihāra viceroy.
Verse 11 of the Udayapur Praśasti hints at Dhārā's recovery; Bühler's reading of 'indicated'.
Siyaka also known as Harṣa; Udayapur Praśasti and Arthuna inscription call him Harṣa, Merutuṅga Simhadantabhaṭa.
Harsola grant of V.S. 1005 (949 A.D.): Siyaka worshipped Śivanātha and granted two villages to Brahmans.

reject_reason: Siyaka's campaigns against Saurastra Calukyas and Hunas; military detail without bearing on the units

items.note: Candella kingdom extended to Bhilsa (Bhāsvat) on the Mālava river by the Khajuraho inscription of 954 A.D.
Dhanapāla's Pāiyalacchī dates the sack of Mānyakheṭa by the lord of Mālava to 971-2 A.D.; Udayapur Praśasti mentions Siyaka's victory over Khoṭṭiga.
Assessment: Paramāras were mainly instrumental in destroying the Rāṣṭrakūṭa empire by sacking Mānyakheta.
Siyaka called the real founder of the Paramāra kingdom; empire extended east to Bhilsa.
Siyaka abdicated for Vākpati as an ascetic; queen Vadajā; another son Sindhurāja; died between 970 and 973 A.D.
Vākpati's first inscription, V.S. 1031 (974 A.D.), from Ujjain, grants a village to the Brahman Vasantācārya.
Vākpati, Muñja and Utpala identified as one king, by Arjunavarman's commentary and the Navasāhasāṅka-carita.
Merutuṅga's story of Muñja found as an infant in muñja grass and adopted by Siyaka.
With Vākpati's accession a new era dawned on Malwa; rulers turned to cultural development and social welfare.
Udayapur praśasti says Vākpati defeated Yuvarāja and established supremacy in Tripurī, corroborated by the Kauthem grant.

reject_reason: Vakpati's Mewar and Marwar campaigns; Udaipur here is Rajasthan; no bearing on Udaypur

items.note: Vākpati divided conquered territory among princes of the Dhārā house: Aranyarāja at Abu, Candana at Jalor, Dūsala at Bhinmal.

reject_reason: Vakpati's wars with Cahamanas, Hunas and Caulukyas; military detail without bearing on units
Padmagupta verses on the Gurjara king Mularaja; no bearing on units

items.note: Udayapur praśasti records Vākpati's victory over the people of Lāta.
Vākpati's extensive conquests, mostly regained by Caulukyas and Kalacuris soon after.
Udayapur praśasti relates Vākpati's victory over the Colas and Keralas.
